clue.text: Support the other child first, an ancient writer

indicators.note: 'other' asks for the neighbouring little word made other than it is, so its letters take a different order

blocks.note: a minor is a person under legal age, a child; 'first' puts it at the front
a prop is a support
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone props up another of their children before the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' overrides clue order, so the child comes ahead of the support. The twelve Minor Prophets are the short Old Testament books from Hosea to Malachi.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelve Minor Prophets, such as Hosea or Amos, are authors of short books of the Old Testament, so ancient writers.

clue.text: What fisherman might have done incorrectly when given unsuitable part

definitions.text: What fisherman might have done incorrectly

blocks.clueFragment: What fisherman might have done incorrectly
blocks.note: first meaning: an angler who throws the line badly has made a poor cast
second meaning: an actor put in a role that does not suit them

explanation.surface: An actor handed the wrong role is compared to a clumsy angler.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the word as MIS (wrongly) + CAST (thrown, of a fishing line).
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre and film use the word for an actor placed in a role that does not suit them.

clue.text: Emperor came from old Northeast Region to start with

indicators.note: what comes at the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the compass abbreviation
the opening letter of the word
O is a standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A Roman ruler is said to have come from some ancient north-eastern territory.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are not used in clue order: NE and R come first and the O for 'old' goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was the Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68, notorious for persecution and the great fire of Rome.

clue.text: Send back to prison the chap overdrawn

indicators.note: read as a person drawn over by something, so the chap sits inside the other word

blocks.note: a chap is a man
an overdrawn account is in the red

explanation.surface: A man who has gone overdrawn is sent back to jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overdrawn' does double duty: it gives RED and says MAN is covered by it, RE(MAN)D.
explanation.definitionFit: A court remands an accused person in custody, returning them to prison to await the next hearing.

clue.text: Again promise to return bill for further consideration

blocks.note: first meaning: commit oneself once more
second meaning: parliamentary procedure for sending a bill back to committee

explanation.surface: A legislator vows once more to send a bill back for another look.
explanation.definitionFit: In parliament, a bill is sent back to a committee for further work; generally, the verb means pledge oneself anew.

clue.text: Penny for a second time distinguished and surpassing others

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny
the prefix meaning again
an eminent person is distinguished

explanation.surface: Someone called Penny wins distinction twice over and outshines everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pre-eminent stands above all rivals, excelling everybody else in its field.

clue.text: Maturer sort of mistake

indicators.note: to sort is to put in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An older person makes a certain kind of error.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is an error in print, usually listed on a correction slip in a book.

clue.text: Seeking hostilities along the way of the expedition

definitions.text: along the way of the expedition

blocks.note: first meaning: angry and spoiling for a fight

blocks.clueFragment: along the way of the expedition
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: travelling the route a war party takes

explanation.surface: An army looks for a fight as it marches along its route.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: a warpath is the track of a warlike expedition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone angry and looking for confrontation, from the war parties of Native American tribes.

clue.text: Quack remedy is no way strange

blocks.note: taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street, a way
rum is British informal for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A doctor declares that a fake cure is not at all peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a patent medicine of doubtful worth, the kind sold by charlatans.

clue.text: Become happier now food is more expensive!

blocks.note: cheer in the old sense of food and drink, as in good cheer
prices that are up are higher

explanation.surface: A wry exclamation about rising food prices.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'food is up', with 'now' and 'is' only joining the pieces into a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheer up is a phrasal verb for growing more cheerful after a gloomy spell.

clue.text: Headline reader

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who reads the headlines in a newspaper
setter's reading: someone who reads the lines and bumps of a person's head

explanation.surface: Someone skimming the front page of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Headline' as head line: the reader studies the contours of the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: Practitioners of the Victorian pseudoscience claimed to judge character by feeling bumps on the skull.

clue.text: Leg-pull, short-cut after half-hour

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, so the second two letters are dropped
a word left short loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: Someone claims a short cut saves half an hour, and it's a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short-cut' looks like a quicker route, but it splits into two jobs: 'cut' gives a word and 'short' docks its last letter. AX is a common American spelling of axe.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoax is a trick or practical joke, which is what pulling someone's leg means.

clue.text: Wind instrument

blocks.note: surface reading: a musical instrument played by blowing, like a flute
setter's reading: a scientific device that measures the wind

explanation.surface: A flute, oboe or trumpet.
explanation.definitionFit: This device, with spinning cups, measures the speed of moving air for weather stations.

clue.text: Idiot, after noon, comin' round on deck

indicators.note: turned round means jumbled about, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for noon
taken as written, dropped g and all
the poop is the raised deck at a ship's stern

explanation.surface: A fool comes wandering round on the ship's deck in the afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: A nincompoop is a foolish or stupid person, an informal word for a simpleton.

clue.text: Trendy comic success

blocks.note: a wit is a comic, someone funny
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A fashionable comedian scores a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated slang for fashionable and up to date, in tune with the latest styles.

clue.text: Wrongdoer said to be supplying Scotsman spice

indicators.note: said to be means spoken, so the sound of the word counts rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a sinner is a wrongdoer; in a non-rhotic accent it matches these letters
mon is the Scots form of man

explanation.surface: A dodgy Scottish spice dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: MON is how a Scotsman says 'man', a fitting nod in a Scotsman crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinnamon is the aromatic bark of a tropical tree, ground or rolled into sticks for cooking.

clue.text: Herbert recollected name of relatives

indicators.note: read as re-collected, gathered up again in a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Herbert remembered what his relations were called.
explanation.definitionFit: Brethren is the old plural of brother, used for kinsmen or members of a fellowship.

clue.text: Fairly stiff programme of course

blocks.note: surface reading: a demanding schedule, naturally
setter's reading: a printed card listing the runners at a racecourse

explanation.surface: Admittedly, the schedule is quite demanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' is not 'naturally' but a racecourse, and 'fairly stiff' describes card rather than a tough task.
explanation.definitionFit: Punters buy this card at the track listing each race, its horses, jockeys and starting times.

clue.text: Group had small cottage on the lake

blocks.note: cot is an old word for a small cottage
Lake Erie, one of the North American Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A set of friends shared a little lakeside cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the cottage goes on top of the lake. Erie is one of North America's Great Lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small exclusive circle of people sharing interests, a clique.

clue.text: Set up in office in last resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An official is appointed as a desperate final measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' looks like a fixed phrase, but 'resort' is the anagram signal. INSTAL is a variant spelling of install.
explanation.definitionFit: To instal someone is to induct them formally into a post or position of authority.

clue.text: Some twenty-two folders? Twice as many

indicators.note: only some of the letters in the following words are used, a run inside them

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the hyphenated number and the next word

explanation.surface: Asking whether twenty-two folders amounts to double the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Something twofold is doubled, having two parts or twice the amount.

clue.text: Name given to Peter during apprentice phase

indicators.note: something happening during a period falls within it, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone acquired a nickname while still training.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Gospels, Jesus gives Simon the Aramaic name Cephas, meaning rock, rendered as Peter in Greek.

clue.text: Another tartan item that's hypothetical stuff

indicators.note: another version of the words is a different arrangement of their letters

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: One more piece of tartan turns out to be imaginary.
explanation.walkthrough: Tartan is the checked woollen cloth of Scottish clans.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists describe matter built of antiparticles; once mostly theoretical, it suits a sci-fi notion of imagined material.

clue.text: Departing losing one medal

indicators.note: a word losing something has a letter taken out of it

blocks.note: going is departing
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone leaves after forfeiting their decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: GOING without the I for 'one' leaves GONG, British slang for a medal or honour.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls a medal or official award a gong, especially a military decoration.

clue.text: Mythological princess performed with love

blocks.note: did is performed
love is zero in tennis, the shape of O

explanation.surface: A legendary princess acted out a love story.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido, queen of Carthage, was a Tyrian princess who loved Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid.

clue.text: Entertain with port

blocks.note: first meaning: hold in the mind, as a thought or grudge
second meaning: a sheltered place where ships dock

explanation.surface: Hosting guests with a glass of fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Port looks like the after-dinner drink served while entertaining, but it is the shipping sense.
explanation.definitionFit: One harbours or entertains a suspicion, and a harbour is a haven for ships.

clue.text: He and I have commonsense that's atrocious!

blocks.note: taken as written
the pronoun taken as written
nous is British informal for practical good sense

explanation.surface: Two people claim sound judgement, and the claim is outrageous.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinous describes a wicked act, utterly shocking and monstrous, like an atrocity.

clue.text: Promise to retain single weapon

blocks.note: to retain is to keep
single means one
a sword is a weapon

explanation.surface: A vow to retain a single blade.
explanation.walkthrough: The breaks fall differently in the answer: KEEP ONE + SWORD reads as KEEP ONE'S WORD.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping one's word means honouring a pledge, doing what was promised.
